title: In every posture
hookLine: walking, standing, sitting, lying down, keep effort alive (Itivuttaka 110)

lines: A GRUDGE AT THE BUS STOP.
cards: Walking to the bus, a grudge shows up. Standing in line for coffee, it's still there. Sitting at your desk, you polish it.

Lying in bed at night, you rehearse what you should have said. Four positions, one thought, carried all day like a stone in a shoe. The body changes posture a hundred times a day; the mind often doesn't.
One discourse near the end of the Itivuttaka walks through exactly those four positions, and asks what you do with a thought like that in each one.

teach.b: Itivuttaka 110 is built like a walk through the day.

teach.h: PUTTING UP WITH IT, OR LETTING IT GO
teach.b: If, while a monk is walking, a thought of sensual craving, ill will or harming arises, and he puts up with it, doesn't drop it, doesn't drive it out, then, the Buddha says, he is called lazy, lacking ardor.
Then the same sentence for standing, for sitting, for lying down awake. Four times, nearly word for word.
Then the other side, four times over: if the thought arises while walking and he doesn't tolerate it, but lets it go, dispels it, ends it, he is called ardent, someone whose effort is alive.

The Pali tradition counts these four as the postures, iriyapatha, literally ways of moving; other suttas use them to mean all the time. Notice what the text does not say. It doesn't say the thought shouldn't arise.
Thoughts of wanting, of anger, of hurting someone come to everyone, monks included. The line is drawn after: do you let it settle in, or see it and set it down?
That's a very different standard from never having the thought at all. And notice why the list repeats.
Practice isn't only for the cushion.
A sitting meditator who spends the walk home nursing a grudge has done one posture out of four.
The closing verse pictures someone who keeps at it, walking or standing, sitting or lying down, and says such a one can reach the highest awakening.

how: Many Buddhist teachers include walking meditation alongside sitting, and some monastic training asks students to keep mindfulness through all four postures, from walking and standing to sitting and lying down.

o: a posture, a way of moving

s: Itivuttaka 110 says a good practitioner never has a harmful thought
the line is drawn after the thought arises: tolerate it, or let it go.
the discourse repeats the same sentence for all four postures
walking, standing, sitting, and lying down awake, each nearly word for word.
the four postures are a way of saying all day and night
other suttas use the same four to mean every moment.

games.q: you're walking, and a thought of ill will toward someone shows up. by Itivuttaka 110's standard, what counts as effort?
o: never having the thought at all.
seeing it and letting it go instead of putting up with it.
waiting until you can sit down to deal with it.
games.why: the text doesn't fault the arising. it calls you ardent for not tolerating it, right there, in whatever posture you're in.

practice: Notice how you're sitting right now: the weight in the seat, the feet on the floor, the hands, and let the spine lift a little, without strain.
Then check the mind the same way: is anything being carried, a worry, a grudge, a wanting?
If something is there, don't fight it; see it, the way you saw your posture, and loosen your grip on it a little, the way you'd loosen your shoulders.

wordCard.voice: Iriyapatha. The four postures, walking, standing, sitting and lying down, in every one of which the sutta asks you not to tolerate a harmful thought.

orig.note: Pali iriyapatha: a posture, literally a way of moving; the four are walking, standing, sitting, lying down.

carryVoice: Your line: effort is alive. The thought may come; what counts is whether you set it down. Day six hundred thirty-three, done.
